title: AI vs hiring a receptionist for restaurant calls
seoTitle: AI vs hiring receptionist for restaurant calls | ROAL
description: Compare AI and hiring a receptionist for restaurant phones: cost, coverage, order taking, and when an AI phone host makes more sense.
question: Should I use an AI phone host or hire someone to answer my restaurant’s phone?
answer: For many independent restaurants, an AI phone host is cheaper and easier to keep on duty than hiring someone just for calls. Hiring makes sense when you want a person on-site for complex guest service, but an AI phone host can handle pickup and delivery orders, hours, menu questions, and reservations, while staff handle tricky calls and payments.
summary: Compare phone costs, coverage, and order flow so you can choose the setup that fits your restaurant.
intro:
An AI phone host is often a better fit than hiring someone just for the phone when most calls are order taking, hours, and simple questions. Hiring a receptionist makes more sense when you need a person at the counter too, or when your calls need constant human judgment.

For a pizza shop, deli, or takeout spot, the real question is not “AI or human?” It is “What do I need this phone to do, how many calls do I get, and what will it cost me each month?”

sections.h2: What do you actually need the phone to do during a rush?
sections.body:
Before you compare costs, write down the job. A restaurant phone can do a few very specific things: take pickup orders, take delivery orders, answer hours and address questions, handle reservations, and route special calls to staff.

A phone host like ROAL can take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from the live menu. It also collects the caller’s name and phone, gives a ready time, and confirms the order back. It does not take card numbers over the phone, and it sends tricky calls like allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering, and manager requests to staff with a summary.

Use this quick checklist:
- Do you mostly get order calls, or lots of “are you open?” calls?
- Do callers ask for toppings, add-ons, and special instructions?
- Do you need multilingual phone help?
- Do you want reservations or catering requests handled too?

Example phone line: “Thanks for calling. What can I get started for pickup or delivery?”

If that is the kind of call you get all day, you need a phone setup built for restaurant work, not a general front desk script.

sections.h2: How does ai vs hiring receptionist compare on cost?
sections.body:
The biggest difference is how you pay.

Many AI phone tools for restaurants charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often somewhere around $79 to $599 whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Hiring a receptionist means payroll, taxes, training, coverage for breaks, and the risk of paying for slow hours.

ROAL uses pay-per-completed-order pricing: $0.90 for each confirmed order whose ticket reaches the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are free.

| Option | Example cost setup | What changes with volume |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly AI plan | $149/month | Cost stays the same even if calls are light |
| Human answering service | per call or per minute | More calls usually means more cost |
| Hired receptionist | hourly pay plus payroll costs | Cost stays steady even on slow days |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed order | You pay only when an order is confirmed |

If your phone mainly brings in orders, pay-per-order can be easier to judge. If your calls are mostly questions, compare the fixed monthly options carefully.

sections.h2: What happens when the phone rings after hours or during the dinner rush?
sections.body:
This is where the difference gets real. A hired receptionist can only answer when someone is on shift. A human service can answer within its own staffing window, but you still pay for that coverage. An AI phone host can stay on the line after hours, during breaks, or when your staff is slammed.

ROAL gets set up from your website, Google Maps link, or even just your restaurant name and city. It reads your menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages, then builds a phone host in about two minutes. The owner can test-call it in the browser before going live, with no sign-up needed.

A practical rush-hour setup looks like this:
1. Let the phone ring normally during calm periods.
2. Forward all calls when the line gets busy, or only unanswered calls.
3. Send order calls to the phone host.
4. Send special cases to staff.

Example line for busy shifts: “Hold on one moment while I place your order.”

If your team is short-staffed, a phone host can cover the routine work while your crew focuses on food and guests.

sections.h2: Which option is better for order accuracy and ticket flow?
sections.body:
A receptionist can be great if that person knows the menu well and stays focused. But in many restaurants, the phone person is also juggling the front counter, walk-ins, and in-house guests. That is where mistakes happen.

An AI phone host is built to follow a menu and ask for the details that matter. It can take item names, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It will not offer items marked sold out. It can also answer questions about menu items, hours, parking, and address, which cuts down on back-and-forth.

Here is a simple comparison for a $28 average order. Plug in your own number:
- If one missed or garbled order is common, the waste can add up fast.
- If a human repeats the order perfectly every time, great.
- If your staff is rushed, a structured phone host may keep the ticket cleaner.

Example script line: “Just to confirm: one large pepperoni, extra cheese, no onions, for pickup under Maria, ready in about 20 minutes.”

That confirmation step matters more than a fancy greeting. Clean tickets save time at the make line and reduce callbacks.

sections.h2: How should you handle weird calls, complaints, and special requests?
sections.body:
No phone setup should try to handle every situation alone. Restaurants get allergy questions, complaints, large catering requests, manager requests, and callers who just want a person.

ROAL is set up to hand those calls to staff with a summary. Questions it cannot answer land in an inbox, and once the owner answers one of them, the host knows it from then on. That makes it better for the repeat questions your store gets all the time.

A useful handoff plan for any restaurant is:
- Let the phone host handle orders, hours, menu, and reservations.
- Send allergy-sensitive questions to staff.
- Send complaints to staff.
- Send catering and manager requests to staff.
- Keep a short internal note for common situations.

Example line for staff handoff: “I’m going to get someone from the store for that.”

If you hire a receptionist, train them to use the same rule. The goal is not to force every call through one person. The goal is to keep the phone moving without giving wrong answers.

sections.h2: What should you choose if you are small, busy, and short-staffed?
sections.body:
For many independent restaurants, the choice comes down to flexibility.

If you only need a person for the phone, hiring can be expensive and hard to cover. If you need help with the host stand, phones, and walk-ins, a person may be worth it. If you mainly want calls answered, orders taken, and routine questions handled, an AI phone host can be the simpler setup.

A quick decision table:
| Situation | Better fit |
|---|---|
| Mostly pickup and delivery orders | AI phone host |
| Need a person on-site for guests | Hired receptionist |
| Large share of after-hours calls | AI phone host |
| Highly complex guest service | Human staff |
| Want pay only when orders come in | ROAL |

ROAL is worth a look if you want a restaurant-specific phone host that can be set up from your public menu and forwarded to your existing number. You keep your own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

sections.h2: How do you set up call forwarding without making a mess?
sections.body:
Good forwarding keeps your current number and sends the calls where they need to go. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your existing number to it. You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered.

The exact code depends on your carrier or phone system, so always confirm with them and test with a real call. Common patterns are:
- Many landlines and some carriers: *72 to forward all calls, *73 to turn it off.
- AT&T and T-Mobile GSM lines: **21*number# for all calls, ##21# off; **61*number# for unanswered calls; **67*number# for busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless: *72 / *73 for all calls, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems: usually set it in the web portal.

A simple rollout plan:
1. Pick one location.
2. Test forwarding during a slow hour.
3. Place a few test calls.
4. Check the ticket on the kitchen screen.
5. Then decide whether to forward all calls or only overflow calls.

That keeps the change low-risk and easy to reverse.

takeaways: Compare the job first: orders, questions, reservations, and handoffs.
Hiring a receptionist adds payroll overhead; AI tools often charge monthly, while ROAL charges per completed order.
Use call forwarding slowly and test it with real calls before turning it on fully.
For restaurants, order accuracy and clean kitchen tickets matter as much as who answers the phone.

faq.q: Is an AI phone host cheaper than hiring a receptionist for a restaurant?
faq.a: Usually yes, especially if you only need phone coverage and not a full front-desk employee. Hiring adds hourly pay, payroll costs, training time, and coverage gaps, while many AI phone tools charge a monthly fee and some charge per order or per call. ROAL charges $0.90 per completed order instead of a monthly fee.

faq.q: Can a restaurant AI phone host take orders from the menu?
faq.a: Yes. ROAL takes pickup and delivery orders from the restaurant’s live menu, including items, sizes, modifiers, and notes. It also collects the caller’s name and phone and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

faq.q: What calls should still go to staff instead of the phone host?
faq.a: Allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests should go to staff. ROAL can hand those calls off with a summary so your team has context before calling back or taking over live.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant number to an AI phone host?
faq.a: You keep your existing number and forward it to the phone host’s line. Many carriers and phone systems use codes like *72, *73, or carrier-specific GSM codes, but the exact method varies, so confirm with your carrier and test a call after setup.
